slides.headline: No renames

slides.headline: No renames

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Edits disappear after git restore <path>. Root cause: the working tree was overwritten from the index, and content that was never staged is in no object.
Expecting git restore <path> to return the last committed version. Root cause: without --source the content comes from the index, which may hold something you staged and forgot.
git restore --source=<old commit> <directory> deletes files. Root cause: restore runs in no-overlay mode, so tracked paths that the source lacks are removed.
The history of a file stops at a rename. Root cause: the rename commit also rewrote the file, and the similarity fell below the threshold; rename and edit in separate commits.
Using git rm --cached to unstage a change. Root cause: it removes the index entry, and the next commit deletes the path for everyone else; it is the tool to stop tracking a file.

beats.text: An engineer has spent an afternoon on a failed experiment. Twenty files are changed, the tests are red, and in frustration they type git restore . at the top of the repository.

beats.text: Nineteen of those changes were worthless. One was the fix for a bug they had found on the way. It's gone. No commit, meaning no saved snapshot of the project, holds it. No reflog, Git's local journal of where your branches pointed, recorded the event. And Git has no undo for it.

The usual trigger is frustration, and the usual loss is the one useful change among twenty useless ones. beats.text: git restore overwrites files with a stored version. git mv and git rm move and remove files, and tell the index in the same step. And then a question that sounds like trivia and isn't: does Git record that a file was renamed? It doesn't. You'll prove that by opening a commit, and you'll see where the word "rename" in Git's output comes from.

beats.text: First, a five-second reminder of three places. The working tree is the files on your disk. The index, or staging area, is Git's list of what goes into the next commit, and git add copies a file into it: that's staging. And HEAD is the last commit.

beats.text: When it is appropriate: after you've read the diff and decided that the changes are worthless. When in doubt, commit to a throwaway branch, or stash, which parks your uncommitted work. Both keep the content.

beats.text: Two choices define a restore. First, where the content comes from. Without --source, that's the index, or HEAD if --staged is given. With --source=<tree>, it's that commit or tree. Second, where it's written. The working tree by default. The index with --staged. Both, when --staged and --worktree are given together.

Second, where it's written. The working tree by default. The index with `--staged`. Both, when `--staged` and `--worktree` are given together.

beats.text: Quick quiz, two options. You staged a change this morning and forgot it. Now you edit the file again, dislike it, and run git restore on it, with no flags. Do you get the last commit, or what you staged? Say your answer.

beats.text: What you staged. Without --source, the content comes from the index. Almost everyone says the last commit the first time, and that's normal.
beats.tele: What you staged. Without `--source`, the content comes from the index. Almost everyone says the last commit the first time, and that's normal.

beats.text: Two details. The command needs at least one pathspec, meaning a path or pattern that selects files. And the default mode is "no overlay": a tracked path that doesn't exist in the source is removed, so that the destination matches the source exactly. That has a sharp edge. git restore --source=HEAD~5 src/ removes every tracked file under src/ that didn't exist five commits ago, together with any unstaged changes in them. So name files, not directories, when you take content from an old commit.

And the default mode is "no overlay": a tracked path that doesn't exist in the source is removed, so that the destination matches the source exactly. That has a sharp edge. `git restore --source=HEAD~5 src/` removes every tracked file under `src/` that didn't exist five commits ago, together with any unstaged changes in them. So name files, not directories, when you take content from an old commit.

beats.text: Inside .git. Restoring the working tree from the index reads the blob that the index entry names, and writes it to disk. A blob is the object that holds one file's content. No object is created, and no ref, meaning no branch name, moves. So no reflog records the event. The content that was overwritten isn't saved anywhere.

No object is created, and no ref, meaning no branch name, moves. So no reflog records the event. The content that was overwritten isn't saved anywhere.

beats.text: What survives. One exception is worth knowing. Anything that was ever staged went into the object database, Git's store inside the dot git folder, when git add ran. git fsck can find it as a dangling blob. Dangling objects are removed by garbage collection, Git's clean-up of unused objects, after a grace period, two weeks by default. So this is a rescue route, not a storage plan.
beats.tele: What survives. One exception is worth knowing. Anything that was ever staged went into the object database, Git's store inside the dot git folder, when `git add` ran. `git fsck` can find it as a dangling blob. Dangling objects are removed by garbage collection, Git's clean-up of unused objects, after a grace period, two weeks by default. So this is a rescue route, not a storage plan.

beats.text: git mv and git rm. In one sentence: they do in one step what you can do in two. You change the working tree with mv or rm, then you tell the index.
beats.tele: `git mv` and `git rm`. In one sentence: they do in one step what you can do in two. You change the working tree with `mv` or `rm`, then you tell the index.

beats.text: git mv <source> <destination> is 🟢 SAFE: it renames the file on disk and renames its index entry. git rm <path> is 🟡 CAUTION: it deletes the file on disk and removes its index entry, and it refuses when the file's content isn't safely stored in HEAD. With -f it overrides that check, and is 🔴 DANGEROUS for that reason. --cached removes only the index entry. Neither command creates a commit. The index is updated, and the change must still be committed.
beats.tele: `git mv <source> <destination>` is 🟢 SAFE: it renames the file on disk and renames its index entry. `git rm <path>` is 🟡 CAUTION: it deletes the file on disk and removes its index entry, and it refuses when the file's content isn't safely stored in HEAD. With `-f` it overrides that check, and is 🔴 DANGEROUS for that reason. `--cached` removes only the index entry. Neither command creates a commit. The index is updated, and the change must still be committed.

beats.text: Two behaviors that the textbook's authors found while writing the demos. git rm deletes a directory when it removes the last file in it. And git mv doesn't create a missing destination directory.

beats.text: No renames. In one sentence: a commit stores a snapshot of paths and contents, so there's no place in it where "this file used to be called that" could be written. A rename is a conclusion that Git draws later, by comparing two snapshots.

beats.text: When a diff, a comparison of two snapshots, is computed, a deleted path and an added path with similar content are reported as a rename, with a similarity score. R100 means 100 percent similar. The default threshold is 50 percent.

beats.text: Why this matters. Three habits follow from detection being a heuristic, a good guess. First, rename in one commit and edit in the next when the edit is large. A rename combined with a rewrite can fall below the threshold, and then git log --follow, git blame and the rename handling in merges all treat it as an unrelated new file.

A rename combined with a rewrite can fall below the threshold, and then `git log --follow`, `git blame` and the rename handling in merges all treat it as an unrelated new file.

beats.text: Second, expect very large moves to look like delete plus add. The exhaustive part of detection is skipped when the number of candidate files exceeds diff.renameLimit, whose default the 2.55 manual gives as 1000. Third, don't look for a "rename" flag to audit. There's none in the data.

The exhaustive part of detection is skipped when the number of candidate files exceeds `diff.renameLimit`, whose default the 2.55 manual gives as 1000. Third, don't look for a "rename" flag to audit. There's none in the data.

beats.text: A picture helps. For git restore, the textbook's analogy is "revert to saved" in an editor, where "saved" means "last staged". It breaks twice. There's no undo afterwards. And "saved" is the index, not the last commit, which surprises people who have staged something and forgotten.

beats.text: For renames, think of two photographs of a room, taken a day apart. In the first, a chair stands by the window. In the second, an identical chair stands by the door, and there's none by the window. You say "someone moved the chair". Nothing in either photograph says so. It's your inference from comparing them. And if the chair had also been repainted, you might have said "someone removed one chair and brought another". The rename is the reader's inference.

beats.text: The entry kept its blob ID and changed its path. git write-tree prints the ID of the tree that this index describes. Remember that ID. The script now undoes everything and performs the rename with shell commands. Predict the tree ID: the same, or different? Say it out loud.

beats.text: The same. The tree ID is identical, beginning 566379b both times. That's the proof that git mv adds nothing that mv plus git add -A doesn't.

beats.text: The word comes from the comparison. R100 means "a deleted path and an added path whose contents are 100 percent similar". Turn detection off with --no-renames, and the same two commits show a deletion and an addition.

beats.text: Rename and edit in one commit: the similarity drops to 96. Raise the threshold to 98 percent, and the rename is no longer reported. So whether you see a rename depends on a threshold.

beats.text: History that follows a file depends on the same detection. Without --follow, the log of src/vector_search.py starts at the commit where that path first appears. With it, Git detects the two renames and continues. --follow works for a single file only.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Edits disappear after git restore <path>. Root cause: the working tree was overwritten from the index, and content that was never staged is in no object.
beats.tele: Edits disappear after `git restore <path>`. Root cause: the working tree was overwritten from the index, and content that was never staged is in no object.

beats.text: Expecting git restore <path> to return the last committed version. Root cause: without --source the content comes from the index, which may hold something you staged and forgot.
beats.tele: Expecting `git restore <path>` to return the last committed version. Root cause: without `--source` the content comes from the index, which may hold something you staged and forgot.

beats.text: git restore --source=<old commit> <directory> deletes files. Root cause: restore runs in no-overlay mode, so tracked paths that the source lacks are removed.
beats.tele: `git restore --source=<old commit> <directory>` deletes files. Root cause: restore runs in no-overlay mode, so tracked paths that the source lacks are removed.

beats.text: The history of a file stops at a rename. Root cause: the rename commit also rewrote the file, and the similarity fell below the threshold; rename and edit in separate commits.
beats.tele: The history of a file stops at a rename. Root cause: the rename commit also rewrote the file, and the similarity fell below the threshold; rename and edit in separate commits.

beats.text: Using git rm --cached to unstage a change. Root cause: it removes the index entry, and the next commit deletes the path for everyone else; it is the tool to stop tracking a file.
